Definition: American Society for Testing Materials — the standards body that defines steel specifications (e.g., A36, A572, A656). When a PO references an ASTM grade, the material must meet those published mechanical and chemical property requirements.
Money owed by customers for goods or services already delivered. Tracked in the ERP system and tied to outstanding invoices.
Extra charges beyond base freight — examples include detention (driver waiting time at a customer dock), fuel surcharges, liftgate fees, and inside delivery charges.
Process of heating and then slowly cooling Hot Rolled and/or Cold Rolled Steel to induce softening of the material. Improves ductility and reduces internal stresses.
Document containing all pertinent information for a specific customer part — essentially the blueprint. Includes size, steel grade, packaging requirements, cost, and processing requirements.
Abrasion-Resistant Steel — a high-hardness steel grade engineered to withstand wear and impact. Used where surfaces are subject to heavy abrasion (e.g., dump truck beds, mining equipment).
Material in inventory that is not reserved or allocated to any existing order — freely available for new sales orders.
Open customer orders that have not yet been produced or shipped. A measure of future workload and capacity demand.

A defect when a strip is cut and the proper nick and break is not achieved — resulting in a rough or irregular edge. Caused by dull knives, improper arbor setting, poor back tension, over-arm separator issues, or other slitter mechanical errors.

A long-term purchase agreement establishing price, grade, and volume over a period (often a year). Individual shipments are called releases. A blanket framework must exist in Invex before release lines can be entered.

A steel-making imperfection produced by gas bubbles — caused by expansion of gas concentrated at a surface inclusion. Appears as small raised areas on the steel surface, either isolated or in longitudinal streaks.

Shipping document issued by the carrier confirming receipt of goods for transport. Serves as a contract between shipper and carrier and is the primary record of material movement. Required content (PO#, bundle weights, etc.) varies by customer.
A third party who arranges transportation between a shipper and a carrier. Does not own trucks — matches loads to available carrier capacity. SWC may use brokers for outbound freight.
Also called center buckle or full center. A flatness defect caused by uneven cooling or poor rolling practice at the mill. Because it is mill-caused, it is claimable against the supplier.

A very subtle ridge on the steel edge left by cutting operations (slitting, trimming, or blanking). Caused by improper clearance at slitters or bad knives, or by improper clearance or a dull shear blade at levelers and shears.
The deviation of a strip edge from a straight line. Standard camber tolerance is 0.250" per 8 feet. Causes include improper slitter alignment, steering issues, or taking too many cuts on the slitter.
Available machine time or processing throughput on a production line or work center. Capacity constraints affect lead times and production scheduling.
The company that physically transports material — trucking companies, railroads, etc. Distinct from a broker, who arranges transport but does not haul.
Used to designate the components of a selling price or costs on a sales order and the purchase price. E.g.: Metal, Freight, Slitting, Packaging.
Charge is the revenue on a sales order; cost represents the actual expenses — including inventory, processing, and freight.
Transverse lines alternately shiny and dull on the surface of slit material. Result of slitting knives slipping, skipping, or poor tension practice during slitting.
Document provided by the mill verifying that the steel meets specified mechanical properties and chemical composition. Required by many customers — must accompany or precede shipment.
Total cost to produce the goods sold in a given period — includes raw material cost, direct labor, and processing overhead. Used in calculating gross margin.
Large rolled steel wound into a cylindrical roll — the primary form in which flat rolled steel is purchased from the mill. SWC processes coils by slitting, leveling, CTL, temper passing, or blast.
Creases or ridges appearing as parallel lines transverse to the rolling direction. Generally extend across the full sheet width. Can result from improper leveling.
A flatness deviation where the entire sheet width arches smoothly — following the curvature it had while wound in the coil. Produced when leveling (flattening) is incomplete.

Flat rolled steel where final thickness was achieved by rolling hot rolled bands at approximately room temperature — without reheating. Produces tighter tolerances and smoother surface than hot rolled.

Export document required for international shipments — details the goods, quantities, declared values, buyer/seller information, and country of origin. Required alongside a USMCA Certificate of Origin for exports to Mexico.
Steel suitable for simple bending or moderate drawing. CQ steel can be bent 180° to lay flat upon itself in any direction at room temperature.
An ongoing customer agreement with pre-negotiated pricing and/or volume commitments. May be a blanket order (with releases) or a standing contract for repeat orders at agreed terms.
Cost per hundredweight (per 100 lbs) — the standard unit used by Steel Warehouse for buying and selling steel. To convert: cost per lb × 100 = cost per cwt. Example: $0.10/lb = $10.00/cwt.
Defines finished goods requirements for a specific customer order — exact size, grade, tolerances, and processing requirements.
Abbreviation for Cold Rolled Steel — processed at room temperature for tighter dimensional tolerances and improved surface finish. See Cold Rolled Steel.
Ragged edges or visible cracks on the edge of slit or sheared material. See also Ragged Edges.

Edge cracks on plate or sheet, sometimes caused by low magnesium in the steel, overheated ingot or slab edges, or burnt edge conditions. Can also result from improper handling or poor slitting practice.
Occur from crowding of metal causing overlap or build-up in the rolling direction or diagonally. Heavy creases can cause splits and are described as open creases.
Correction process for invoice pricing errors. A credit memo cancels or reduces an incorrect invoice; a rebill issues the corrected charge. Both require documentation and approval.
Flatness deviation in the transverse direction — sometimes called "canoeing" when edges are higher than the center. Measured perpendicular to the rolling direction.
Kinking or breaking of a sheet caused by wrapping on too small a diameter. Also known as fluting or paneling. Can be prevented by temper rolling before bending.
A condition where the center of the coil is thicker than the edges. Present on all coils to some degree — a normal characteristic of the rolling process.
Processing operation that uncoils steel and cuts it into flat sheets of a specified length. One of the primary services performed by Steel Warehouse.
The acceptable dimensional variation allowed on cut steel. For example, a length tolerance of -0/+¼" means no undercut is acceptable but a slight over-length is fine.
Repetitive impressions in the sheet surface — concave on one side and convex on the other. Result from foreign matter on a roll being pressed into the surface during processing.
A double fracture of material caused by slitting knives set too close together. Visible as a parallel double crease or break line.
Steel with greater ductility and more consistent performance than CQ. Produced to higher standards — used for applications requiring moderate-to-deep drawing.
Drawing Quality steel killed (de-oxidized, typically with aluminum) to prevent aging and increase formability. Used when DQ does not provide sufficient ductility or freedom from aging is required.
Average number of days to collect payment after a sale. A key A/R performance metric — lower DSO means faster cash collection.
The ability of steel to change shape without fracturing. In steel, ductility is typically measured by elongation percentage, yield strength, and tensile strength.
Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization — a measure of core operational profitability before financing costs and non-cash accounting adjustments.
Short creases extending inward from the side edge of temper-rolled sheet — found where extreme edges are substantially thinner and not adequately worked during temper rolling.
Similar to center buckle, but occurs in one or both edges of the strip, generally confined to a narrow portion near the edge.

Mill edge: produced in hot rolling — does not conform to a defined contour, wider width tolerance. Cut edge: produced by shearing, slitting, or trimming — tighter width tolerance and cleaner edge. Cold rolled is typically furnished cut edge; hot rolled can be either.

An additional field — besides form, grade, size, and finish — available when defining a product. There is no Inventory Forecasting functionality by EF. E.g., the product may be defined with a finish of painted and the EF may be the paint color.
The amount of extension a test sample undergoes before fracturing during tensile testing — expressed as a percentage of the original gauge length. A direct measure of ductility.
All the reference tables required to create the STRATIX database.
Integrated software system managing business processes including sales orders, purchasing, inventory, production, and shipping. Invex is the ERP system used by Steel Warehouse.
Expected delivery or pickup time for an inbound or outbound shipment.
Switches added to programs to make them behave differently based on site requirements. Also used to provide default values in certain applications.
Completed, processed material ready for shipment to a customer. Distinct from WIP (Work in Process) or RM (Raw Material).
Remaining coil weight after the primary order quantity has been processed. The fillout may return to inventory or be offered to another customer.
The STRATIX Financial Reporting package for the General Ledger.
A defect where the area near the edge of a partially reduced slab elongates more than the center — resulting in a U-shaped tail end. Seen on all hot roll coils to some degree.

A measure of a cut-to-length sheet's ability to conform to a flat horizontal surface. Maximum deviation from the surface is the degree to which the sheet is out of flat. Customers often specify flatness requirements (e.g., max 0.375" in any 3' span).
Occur when a sheet is pinched and bent over on itself. Transverse to the rolling direction. Occur during subsequent processing operations, not at the mill.
The cost of transportation for a shipment. May be prepaid by SWC (built into price) or collect (customer arranges and pays directly), depending on the freight terms stated on the PO.
Teardrop-shaped marks from excessive changes in coil tension causing laps to slide over one another. Caused by bands breaking, loosely wrapped coils, or more likely on pickle-dry material.
Galvanized steel — steel coated with zinc to prevent corrosion, applied by hot-dipping in molten zinc.
Abbreviation for galvanized steel. See GA / Galvanized.
The thickness of steel — typically expressed in decimal inches (e.g., .250") or gauge numbers for thinner cold rolled products.
A surface scratch or gouge recognizable by its origin — if it occurred in the hot strip mill, rust will have formed at the base; if at the finishing end, the base appears bright.
Hardness measures a material's resistance to permanent deformation. At Steel Warehouse, the primary method is Rockwell Testing — the Rockwell B scale is most commonly used for hot rolled steel.
A surface marking that occurred during mill operations but was subsequently partially removed during later rolling operations. May still be visible as a faint line.
A unique identifier assigned to a specific batch (heat) of steel produced at the mill. Used for traceability — links finished product back to the original mill heat and its test report/cert.

A light pattern of red oxide on the steel surface, usually heavier on the topside. A form of rolled-in scale caused by the steel being too hot after passing through mill hydraulic sprays. Cannot be removed as it is rolled into the surface.
Hot Rolled Steel — processed at high temperatures (above the recrystallization temperature). Has a scaled, rougher surface and looser tolerances than cold rolled, but is generally less expensive.

Hot rolled steel that has had its mill scale removed by pickling (acid bath) and then oiled for surface protection. Better surface quality than standard HR; used where a cleaner surface is needed without full cold rolling.

High Strength Low Alloy steel — achieves increased mechanical properties and atmospheric corrosion resistance through small amounts of alloying elements. Includes grades like A572, A656, and NuStrength Gr100. Handle carefully — no flame cutting or torch straightening.

The application used to adjust products in STRATIX. Adjustments may have financial implications or may involve changing specifications of the material. When financial implications exist, the posting goes to an adjustment account.
Particles of non-metallic material (usually rust, sulfides, silicates, or dirt) entrapped mechanically or formed during solidification or subsequent reaction within the solid steel.
Categorizes inventory into specific types defined by STRATIX: Master, Drop, Finished Good, WIP, Reject, and Scrap. Serves many purposes from costing to reporting.
Bill sent to the customer requesting payment. For toll orders, the invoice covers processing fee only — no material charge, since the customer owns the steel.
After a Transport is updated, STRATIX automatically creates an invoice in edit stage. It is reviewed and finalized using the Invoice Entry function.
Accrual costs based on material receipts, inbound and outbound common carrier freight, and outside processing. When bills are vouchered, they are matched against the associated IRC and cleared.
Supply chain strategy where delivery is timed as closely as possible to when the customer needs the material — minimizing their inventory holding. Requires reliable lead times.
A set of processes that, when combined, produce a finished product. Examples: Pick, Slit, Package, Saw, Drill, Burn, Paint at an Outside Processor.
Steel de-oxidized by silicon or aluminum to minimize oxygen content, preventing reaction during solidification. Has more uniform properties and chemical composition. See also DQSK.
A quantifiable metric used to evaluate performance against a goal. Examples in steel operations: on-time delivery %, DSO, yield %, machine utilization.
Internal imperfections resulting from blisters, seams, or foreign inclusions — sometimes visible on the surface. Related to Slivers. Can cause issues in cutting, welding, or forming.
Process of cutting steel to a specified size using a high-powered laser. Achieves tighter tolerance than slitting or leveling — typically ±0.005". Used for precision parts.
Time elapsed from placement of an order to receipt or delivery. Includes mill lead time (purchased material) or in-house processing time (service center orders).
Running coiled steel through a multi-roll leveler to produce flat sheet. The rolls flex and stretch the steel to remove coil set and other flatness defects.

A Lift groups products together tagged with a lift tag number — individual components retain their identity in Stock Available, and the Lift tag is scanned during shipping Load Verification. A Package combines like items (from the same SO and line item) onto a single tag — individual tags are consumed to create the Packaging tag, which shows in Stock Available. Most commonly used with the slitting process and Production Weight Recording.
Finalizing a shipment record in Invex — confirming the carrier, pickup date, and load details. Triggers BOL generation.
A group of material processed together in the same production run under the same conditions. Lot traceability links finished goods back to their source coil and mill cert.
Decision of whether to produce material for a specific incoming order (make-to-order) or pull from existing finished goods inventory (stock). Affects lead time and inventory levels.
Profit remaining after subtracting cost of goods sold from revenue. Gross margin = revenue − COGS. A key measure of pricing effectiveness.
Material that does not meet specified requirements (grade, dimensions, surface quality, etc.). Must be dispositioned — returned to supplier, reworked, sold as secondary, or scrapped.
The application for recording credit notes and customer returns. The vendor side is reserved for future implementation.

A processing-fee order where the customer owns the raw material and SWC performs an operation (slit, level, CTL, temper pass, blast, etc.) for a fee. Material is not traced to specific customer part numbers. No material purchase in Invex; invoice is for processing only.
Bright, smooth, oval spots on the steel surface — result from oil accidentally dripped or splashed onto a roll or sheet and then leveled into the surface.
Application of a thin coat of oil to flat rolled steel to retard surface rusting. Provides short-term protection — not a fabrication lubricant. Common on CR and HRPO products.

Spans all of STRATIX — a combination of the Sales Order, the Line Item, and the Release. STRATIX supports multiple releases per sales order item (e.g., different due dates). When Production Planning, it is necessary to plan down to the release level.
On Hand = total physical inventory at the plant. Available = on-hand minus material already reserved to existing orders. Only Available inventory can be committed to new orders.
Processing of material at a non-company-owned facility. Also used to refer to an OP warehouse.
A coarse surface texture resembling orange skin — becomes evident during drawing. Caused by excessively large grain size in the steel.

Unintentional side-to-side shifting of a coil while being wound at the mill or during recoiling. Caused by poor coil shape, bad pickler tracking, or slitter misalignment — results in telescoped or offset coil wraps.
The difference between two diagonal measurements of a rectangular sheet, or deviation from 90° at sheet corners. Material is out-of-square when opposite diagonal measurements differ.
Producing more (over run) or less (under run) than the ordered quantity. Tolerance is typically stated on the PO or governed by standard industry practice.
Hot rolled steel that has been pickled (scale removed) and oiled (surface protected). Cleaner surface than standard HR.
A factor used to calculate theoretical coil weights and sizes. Multiplying P.I.W. by coil width gives weight per lineal foot — useful for estimating coil length and yield.

Used to make financial adjustments to products where the original IRC needs an associated entry for reconciling. E.g., a PO is entered, material is received with an incorrect price, the bill comes in and does not match the IRC — a PCA adjusts the price and an adjusting IRC is created.

An Enterprise Parameter that determines how material is costed after production is recorded, based on process and inventory type. E.g., Master Returns go back at the Cost of Consumption and Finished Goods get scrap prorated into the cost.
Provides a business or product management-oriented view of STRATIX Product to track performance and manage the business.
Removal of mill scale or surface oxide by immersing steel in a dilute acid solution (sulfuric or hydrochloric), then rinsing and drying. Often followed by oiling for long-term surface protection.
Fern-like ripples or creases running diagonally to the rolling direction on flat rolled products.
Separation between the surfaces of flat rolled products caused by oxide inclusions originating from the pipe (hollow center) of the original ingot.
Depressions in the surface of a sheet or strip. A common defect. Clearly visible when pickling off rust or rolled-in scale. Less likely on material stored indoors.

A formal order document. In SWC context: (1) a customer's PO to SWC for steel or processing services, or (2) SWC's PO to a mill or supplier for raw material. The PO number is a key reference on all related documents.
Defines the raw material specs (coil specs) purchased from the mill — including grade, dimensions, chemistry, and surface requirements.
Speeds up the Purchase Order entry process for often-repeated product purchases and minimizes user errors.
An expected inbound material record created in Invex before the coil physically arrives. Allows production planning to schedule work in advance of delivery.

Assigned when setting up the Process EP in STRATIX. Each Process Class has programming that allows the consumption of one product to produce another. Examples include Assembly, Burning, Cut to Length, Inspection, Slitting, and Sawing. There are 26 Process Classes in STRATIX in total.
A series of processes entered on a Sales Order required to produce a finished good. The Process Route is pulled into a Job Set for production.

Used in STRATIXview to provide options for searching for material. Default is by Form, Grade, Size, Finish, and Dimension. With Free Form, these fields are entered with a space after each, then the dimension. Product Access codes are defined from the Product Enterprise Parameter and used as shortcuts to search for inventory.
The system order used to authorize and execute a manufacturing operation (slitting, leveling, CTL, etc.) against a sales order. Ties the job to the coil, work center, and routing.
Defines what must be done to material to make it a finished good. E.g., Sawing, Slitting, Cut to Length.
The actual machines used to perform a process.
A machine or group of machines with like processing capabilities.
The broader process and systems used to ensure products consistently meet specified standards — includes procedures, audits, and documentation. Preventive in nature.
Inspection and testing of material to verify it meets spec — measurement of actual dimensions, surface inspection, mechanical testing. Detective in nature.
A group of properties made up of actual Chemical, Physical, and Mechanical properties related to either a Mill-Heat or one or more Product Items.
A pricing offer made to a customer for a specific quantity of material or processing service. Not a binding order until a PO is received and a Sales Order is entered in Invex.

Edges that are torn, split, cracked, or otherwise disfigured. Can be caused by chemistry/heating practice, poor slitting, or annealing damage. Also known as cracked edges, saw-tooth edges, or torn edges.
Reducing the thickness of a sheet or strip by hot or cold rolling. Each pass reduces thickness by a percentage — multiple passes may be required to reach the target gauge.
Transverse breaks or ridges on successive inner laps of a coil. Result from crimping the lead end into a segmented gripping mandrel or from excessive coiling tension.
A specific delivery demand pulled against an existing blanket or contract order. Each release specifies quantity, size, and required ship date against the pre-established contract terms.
Making an order available to production planning in Invex — signals the order is confirmed and ready to be scheduled on a machine.
An internal request to purchase material — submitted by operations or sales to Purchasing to initiate a buy from a mill or supplier.
Assigning specific material (by tag number or heat) to an open sales order. Once reserved, that material is not available for other orders.
Material assigned to a specific sales order. Appears in On-Hand inventory count but is not Available for other orders.
Unprocessed material — typically coils as received from the mill — before any slitting, leveling, CTL, or other processing.

A hardness test where a diamond cone or hardened steel ball is forced into a sample under a standard load. Depth of penetration indicates hardness. The Rockwell B scale is most commonly used for hot rolled steel at SWC.
A repetitive roll mark appearing as a raised spot thicker than the surrounding sheet. Usually caused by a shear burr, scrap, or foreign object indenting a work roll.
A repetitive indentation pattern on steel caused by a foreign substance attached to a work roll. Once the substance is removed, residual roll damage can cause Roll Bruising on subsequent material.
Dark streaks in the rolling direction caused by surface scale (oxide) being rolled into the steel. Can be caused by a leveler or temper mill when excessive scale exists.
Return on Net Assets — a profitability metric measuring how efficiently the company generates profit from its assets. EBIT divided by net assets.
The defined sequence of production steps (operations and work centers) required to process a specific order from raw material through finished goods.
A code assigned to a sales order item indicating the type of sale: As Is, Processed, Buyout, Direct Shipment, Scrap, Toll, or Consignment.
Organizations that set published industry standards for Chemistries and Mechanical properties based on the material.
An elongated patch of loosened metal rolled into the steel surface. Caused by steel splashing from the casting stool at the start of a pour and sticking to the mold walls.
The iron oxide layer forming on steel's surface when heated (e.g., during hot rolling). Must be removed by pickling or shot blasting for many applications. Rolled-in scale is a common surface defect.
Material lost or removed during processing — trim ends, defective portions, or unusable remnants. For toll orders, scrap belongs to the customer since they own the material.
An un-welded fold on the steel surface appearing as a crack. Closed seams are light-colored; open seams are dark (oxidized). Usually results from a defect in casting or rolling.

Abrasive surface treatment where steel shot (small metallic particles) is propelled at high velocity against the workpiece to clean, de-scale, or texture the surface. Used by SWC on John Deere bars as a processing service — different from coil toll (slit/level/CTL) since the process is surface treatment, not dimensional cutting.
A recognized coding system designed by the U.S. government to identify the type of business performed by a company.
A defect parallel to the sheet surface appearing as a surface rupture — caused by inclusions separating the surface layer during rolling. Also known as slivers.
A semi-finished steel block with an oblong cross section (width at least twice the thickness). The mill hot- or cold-reduces slabs to the required gauge and ships them as master coils.
Process of cutting coil products to a specified width (or removing edges) using rotary knives. Produces multiple narrower coils (slit mults) from a single master coil.
A confirmed customer order entered into Invex. The SO drives production, inventory reservation, shipping, and invoicing. Created upon receipt of a customer PO.

A toll processing order where finished pieces are traced to specific customer part numbers (e.g., Valmont RP0xxxx). Customer owns the material; SWC invoices processing fee only. Differs from non-specific toll: material is traced by customer part number, finished pieces are labeled with customer part numbers, and export documentation may be required.

The Spec window is used in purchasing and sales to define the tolerances acceptable for width, length, and thickness, as well as maximum weight per piece and skid. Chemical and physical tolerances may also be defined in addition to Metal Standards. For sales, Execution Options may be defined to assure the applied material meets Metal Standards before it is available for shipment.
A one-time, non-contract sale — no blanket order or long-term pricing agreement. Each spot sale is transacted independently at current market pricing.
An Enterprise Parameter that allows a string of processes to be defined that will yield a finished good. Input when a sales order is entered, eliminating the need to manually enter each process.
The source of raw material — typically a steel mill (e.g., SSAB, Nucor, ArcelorMittal) or a distributor. Mill POs are entered in Invex Purchasing.
A unique identifier assigned to a specific piece or coil of material in inventory. Used for traceability — links the physical material to its mill cert, PO, and customer order.
Assigning specific material tags (by tag number) to a sales order — ensuring that exact coil or piece is held for that order and not used elsewhere.

A light cold-rolling pass applied to steel under high pressure to compress, flatten, elongate, and improve the shape (flatness) and surface finish of the steel. One of the primary processing services at SWC.
The maximum stress a material can withstand before it begins to visibly fracture — measured in KSI. The point at which the metal cross section will no longer stretch when pulled.

Mill-provided certification confirming that a specific heat of steel meets the required chemical composition and mechanical properties. Required by most customers — must match the heat number on the material.

Weight calculated from steel dimensions and standard density formulas rather than by scale. Used when actual weight is not measured — common for plate and bar invoicing. Formula: thickness (in) × width (in) × length (in) × density factor.
The specified limits of acceptable deviation from a nominal dimension. For example, a thickness tolerance of ±0.005" means the material can be 0.005" above or below the target and still be in-spec.
Used on Sales Orders and Purchase Orders — made up of the Payment Terms and Discount Terms.
Enterprise Parameter indicating the party responsible for paying Freight on an order, purchase, shipment, or invoice transaction.
Creating a shipment record in Invex — assigns carrier, pickup date, and groups the sales orders being shipped together. Precedes load confirmation and BOL generation.
The shipment grouping in Invex that combines one or more sales orders onto a single truck or pickup. The transport record drives BOL creation and tracks outbound shipment status.

United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement — replaced NAFTA in 2020. A USMCA Certificate of Origin is required for exports of qualifying goods to Mexico or Canada to receive preferential tariff treatment. Required on all Valmont Industries shipments to their Apodaca, Mexico plant.
Associated with an overseas shipment. In STRATIX, it can be used in the Material Transfers application and the Receiving application to associate shipping expenses when vouchering.

A condition where the edges of the steel strip are longer than the center, causing the edges to appear wavy or buckled. Caused by worn work rolls, damaged edges, or poor temper mill / leveler operation.
Thin, shiny, hair-like pieces of steel on the edge of slit material. Caused by over-arm separators positioned too close together during slitting.
Material currently being processed on the production floor — no longer raw material but not yet finished goods. In Invex, WIP tracks material through each routing step.
An internal operations document containing the detailed picking and processing instructions and specifications required for a Job. Each document contains information for one Job.
A specific machine or production line in the plant (e.g., slitter, leveler, CTL line, temper mill, shot blast machine). Work centers are assigned capacity and routing steps in Invex.
The ratio of output material to input material in a processing operation — expressed as a percentage. Yield losses include trim scrap, defects, and rejects.

The stress level (in KSI) at which steel permanently deforms — the point at which it will no longer return to its original shape when the load is removed. Distinct from Tensile Strength (fracture point). A key specification for structural and HSLA grades.
